bark_profile: Smooth grey with raised resin blisters
pest_resistance: Balsam woolly adelgid
soil_preference: Cool, moist, acid; shallow-rooted
description: The Christmas-tree scent of Vermont's north woods. Flat needles with two white bands beneath, and blisters of fragrant resin on smooth grey bark.
fun_fact: Its resin, sold as Canada balsam, was the standard cement for microscope slides and lenses — it bends light almost exactly as glass does, so a glued joint all but disappears.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, becoming thick and furrowed
pest_resistance: Few in the Northeast; better in heat than most firs
soil_preference: Well-drained; more drought tolerant than other firs
description: A western fir with long, blue-grey needles that curve upward from the twig. Tolerates city conditions better than most firs.
fun_fact: Crush a needle and it smells distinctly of lemon, which is the quickest way to tell this fir from a spruce in a planting.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with resin blisters
pest_resistance: Poorly adapted to the Northeast; balsam woolly adelgid
soil_preference: Cool, moist, well-drained
description: A Pacific Northwest fir whose needles lie in flat, glossy ranks and smell strongly of citrus when crushed.
fun_fact: Crushed needles smell of orange peel. It is the tallest of the true firs, reaching well over 200 feet in the Pacific Northwest.

bark_profile: Smooth dark grey, becoming plated
pest_resistance: More heat tolerant than most firs
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; shelter from wind
description: A dense, dark fir from the Caucasus, widely grown for Christmas trees because its needles hold on so stubbornly.
fun_fact: Europe's favourite Christmas tree, because the needles stay on for weeks after cutting. Named for Alexander von Nordmann, who found it in the Caucasus.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking in irregular patches with age
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates urban conditions
description: A small Asian maple with three-lobed leaves like a duck's foot and flaking, patchy bark on older trunks.
fun_fact: One of the classic bonsai subjects: it takes hard pruning without sulking, and old specimens develop flaking, mottled bark in miniature.

bark_profile: Corky, finely fissured, often with ridged twigs
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates alkaline soil and pruning
description: A compact European maple with small, blunt-lobed leaves and milky sap in the leaf stalk. Long used for hedging in Britain.
fun_fact: The traditional maple of English hedgerows, which is why it tolerates shearing better than any other maple.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, becoming lightly furrowed
pest_resistance: Few problems; self-seeds readily
soil_preference: Adaptable; tolerates cold and drought
description: A shrubby maple from northeast Asia grown for its fiercely red autumn colour and fragrant spring flowers.
fun_fact: Among the first trees on campus to turn, going scarlet in early September. Unusually for a maple, the flowers are fragrant.

bark_profile: Cinnamon-orange, peeling in papery curls year round
pest_resistance: Few known problems; slow to establish
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; dislikes drought
description: Cinnamon-coloured bark peels in papery curls year-round, making this small Chinese maple as striking in winter as in leaf.
fun_fact: Most of its seed is empty — viable embryos are rare — so nearly every paperbark maple in cultivation was grafted or grown from a painstakingly sorted batch.

bark_profile: Corky, deeply furrowed grey-brown, unusual for a maple
pest_resistance: Few serious problems; tolerates urban stress well
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates clay and drought once established
description: A tough Japanese maple grown as a street tree for its corky, deeply furrowed bark — unusual in a genus known for smooth grey trunks.
fun_fact: Named for Kingo Miyabe, the Japanese botanist who first described Hokkaido's flora. It is uncommon in the wild and rarer still in gardens.

bark_profile: Pale grey-brown, shallowly ridged
pest_resistance: Boxelder bug; weak wood and frequent breakage
soil_preference: Wet to dry; colonises disturbed ground
description: An untidy, fast-growing native maple with compound leaves that look more like ash. Colonises riverbanks and disturbed ground.
fun_fact: The only maple with compound leaves, which fools almost everyone until they see the paired samaras.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-green, striated when young
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt; scorch in exposed sites
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; shelter from wind
description: The Japanese maple of gardens, with finely cut, star-shaped leaves and a layered, sculptural habit.
fun_fact: More than a thousand named forms have been selected over four centuries of Japanese cultivation, differing in leaf shape, colour and size.

bark_profile: Grey-black with fine regular ridges
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt; girdling roots are common
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates compaction and shade
description: Widely planted street tree now considered invasive in the Northeast; shades out native seedlings.
fun_fact: Snap a leafstalk and it bleeds milky white sap. Sugar maple's runs clear — the fastest way to tell a native from this invasive.

bark_profile: Grey-black with fine regular ridges
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt; girdling roots are common
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates compaction and shade
description: A narrow upright form of Norway maple, planted where a street is too tight for a full crown. Invasive in Vermont like the species.
fun_fact: Snap a leafstalk and it bleeds milky white sap, like every Norway maple; sugar maple's runs clear.

bark_profile: Grey-black with fine regular ridges
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt; dark foliage scorches in heat
soil_preference: Adaptable; tolerates compaction
description: A Norway maple selection whose leaves stay deep purple-black all summer. Invasive like the species, and heavily planted before that was understood.
fun_fact: Purple leaves hold less working chlorophyll than green ones, so this selection grows noticeably slower than the ordinary Norway maple it came from.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, green-tinged on young stems
pest_resistance: Few problems; needs shelter from afternoon sun
soil_preference: Moist, acidic, well-drained; dislikes drought
description: The hardiest of the fine-textured Asian maples, with deeply cut leaves that turn fire-engine red. Survives where Japanese maple will not.
fun_fact: A Korean near-twin of the Japanese maple that shrugs off winters which would kill it — the reason it is planted this far north.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey when young, breaking into shaggy plates
pest_resistance: Generally trouble-free; leafhopper and gall mites cosmetic
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry; tolerates poor drainage
description: One of the earliest trees to flower in spring; tolerant of wet soils.
fun_fact: Red in every season: scarlet flowers before the leaves, red leafstalks all summer, red samaras, red autumn. One of the most widespread trees in eastern North America.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey when young, breaking into shaggy plates
pest_resistance: Generally trouble-free; leafhopper and gall mites cosmetic
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry; tolerates poor drainage
description: Tightly columnar red maple, barely wider than a lamp post at maturity. Fall colour runs orange rather than the scarlet of the species.
fun_fact: Bred for streets and narrow strips: it reaches full height on a footprint barely wider than a lamp post.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey when young, breaking into shaggy plates
pest_resistance: Generally trouble-free; leafhopper and gall mites cosmetic
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry; tolerates poor drainage
description: An upright red maple holding a narrow oval crown without pruning.
fun_fact: A red maple that grows up rather than out, for planting where a spreading crown would meet a building.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey, plating with age
pest_resistance: Generally trouble-free; colours late, sometimes after the first hard frost
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates wet ground
description: A red maple holding glossy foliage late and turning deep crimson well after most maples have dropped.
fun_fact: Holds its leaves and colours late — often still crimson when other red maples are bare, which is where the name comes from.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey when young, breaking into shaggy plates
pest_resistance: Generally trouble-free; better street tolerance than the straight species
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry; tolerates poor drainage
description: A red maple selection chosen for early, reliable scarlet autumn colour and a strong central leader. One of the most planted street trees in the Northeast.
fun_fact: Colours earlier and more reliably than most red maples, which is why it became one of the most planted street trees in America.

bark_profile: Silver-grey, shaggy and flaking in long strips
pest_resistance: Brittle wood fails in storms; prone to included bark
soil_preference: Wet to moist; very tolerant of flooding
description: Leaves flash silver-white beneath in a breeze, which is where the name comes from. Fast-growing and brittle, so old specimens often carry storm damage.
fun_fact: The pale undersides flash silver when wind turns the leaves, a reliable sign of coming rain. It grows faster than any other maple, and its limbs break accordingly.

bark_profile: Silver-grey, shaggy and flaking in long strips
pest_resistance: Brittle wood fails in storms; prone to included bark
soil_preference: Wet to moist; very tolerant of flooding
description: A cutleaf silver maple whose leaves are dissected almost to the midrib, giving the whole crown a lacy, fern-like texture.
fun_fact: A cutleaf silver maple: the same fast, brittle tree as the species, with leaves dissected almost to the midrib.

bark_profile: Grey, becoming deeply furrowed into long irregular plates
pest_resistance: Sensitive to road salt, compaction and drought — the usual urban decline
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained; dislikes compaction
description: Vermont's state tree and the source of maple syrup. Brilliant orange to scarlet fall color.
fun_fact: It takes about forty gallons of sap to boil down to one gallon of syrup — and a tree needs forty years before it is worth tapping.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: A maple recorded without a species. Vermont's most-planted genus, spanning natives like sugar and red maple and introductions like Norway maple.
fun_fact: A maple seed is a wing with a weight on the end. It autorotates as it falls, and that spin can carry it a hundred yards from the parent tree.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown, becoming lightly ridged
pest_resistance: Few problems; seeds freely enough to escape cultivation
soil_preference: Undemanding; tolerates dry and alkaline soils
description: Small and multi-stemmed, with showy red winged seeds in midsummer that read as flowers from a distance.
fun_fact: Its summer samaras turn bright red and hang in clusters, making a far better show than the small greenish flowers did.

bark_profile: Shaggy, vertically peeling brown, exfoliating in papery strips
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, slightly acidic
description: Named for its flowers in threes. Grown for peeling amber bark and reliably brilliant orange-red fall colour.
fun_fact: Flowers come in threes, which names it. The bark peels in vertical strips and the autumn colour is among the best of any maple.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly ridged with age
pest_resistance: Few known problems; good heat and drought tolerance
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought and alkaline soil
description: A compact Asian maple with glossy, sharply lobed leaves that emerge reddish and turn orange-red. Increasingly planted where larger maples will not fit.
fun_fact: From northern China, where it tolerates heat and drought that would finish a sugar maple — increasingly planted for that reason.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, breaking into plates earlier than red maple
pest_resistance: Better structure than silver maple but still storm-prone if unpruned
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry
description: A hybrid of red and silver maple that combines the red's autumn colour with the silver's speed. Nearly all campus specimens are named cultivars.
fun_fact: A cross between red and silver maple, first made deliberately by Oliver Freeman at the US National Arboretum in 1933. It also happens naturally where the two overlap.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, breaking into plates earlier than red maple
pest_resistance: Better structure than silver maple but still storm-prone if unpruned
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry
description: Columnar Freeman maple, as narrow as the red maple of the same name but faster and more tolerant of poor soil.
fun_fact: A columnar Freeman maple, combining red maple's autumn colour with silver maple's speed in a shape narrow enough for a street.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, plating earlier than red maple
pest_resistance: Fast growth gives weak branch unions — needs structural pruning early
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry; very adaptable
description: A red and silver maple hybrid combining the silver's speed with the red's autumn colour. Widely planted, and widely over-planted.
fun_fact: The most planted Freeman maple anywhere: red maple's colour on silver maple's growth rate, which is a hard combination to argue with.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, plating with age
pest_resistance: Better branch structure and less storm breakage than Autumn Blaze
soil_preference: Wide range, wet to dry
description: A Minnesota-bred Freeman maple with a stronger central leader than Autumn Blaze, and a softer orange-burgundy autumn.
fun_fact: Selected in Minnesota for cold that kills less hardy Freeman maples, with a more natural crown than Autumn Blaze.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking in irregular plates
pest_resistance: Leaf blotch and scorch are routine by late summer; leaf miner
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, deep
description: Big palmate leaves, candelabra flower spikes in May, and the glossy brown conkers that children have collected for centuries.
fun_fact: The conkers are not chestnuts and are mildly poisonous — this tree is not remotely related to the sweet chestnut whose name it borrowed.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, becoming scaly with age
pest_resistance: More leaf-blotch resistant than common horsechestnut
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained
description: A hybrid horsechestnut raised at the Arnold Arboretum, holding its foliage cleanly through a summer that scorches its parents.
fun_fact: Raised at the Arnold Arboretum in Boston, which is where the name comes from.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking in irregular plates
pest_resistance: Much less leaf blotch and scorch than common horsechestnut
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, deep
description: A horsechestnut hybrid with deep rose-red flower spikes and cleaner summer foliage than its European parent.
fun_fact: A hybrid of the common horsechestnut and North America's red buckeye, which is where the pink flowers come from.

bark_profile: Smooth dark grey, marked with pale horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Few problems; fixes its own nitrogen
soil_preference: Wet to average; thrives where drainage is poor
description: Fixes nitrogen at its roots and tolerates soil too wet for most street trees. Small woody cones persist through winter.
fun_fact: Alders host bacteria in root nodules that pull nitrogen straight from the air, so they colonise raw ground that would starve most trees.

bark_profile: Smooth dark grey with prominent lenticels
pest_resistance: Few problems; more heat-tolerant than other alders
soil_preference: Tolerates both wet ground and urban drought
description: A vigorous hybrid alder with long glossy leaves, planted where a tough narrow tree is needed on difficult ground.
fun_fact: Like all alders it fixes its own nitrogen, and it holds its leaves green into late autumn long after most trees have given up.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with darker vertical striping
pest_resistance: Rust and leaf spot in damp years
soil_preference: Moist, acidic; tolerates wet feet better than other serviceberries
description: A suckering, multi-stemmed serviceberry of damp ground. Early white flowers, edible June berries, and orange-red fall colour.
fun_fact: Called shadblow because it flowers when the shad run upriver to spawn — a piece of calendar older than any almanac.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with distinct darker vertical striping
pest_resistance: Rust and leaf spot in wet springs; otherwise easy
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; sun to part shade
description: New leaves emerge bronze-purple beneath a haze of white flowers. The June berries are among the best wild fruit in the Northeast, if the birds leave any.
fun_fact: The berries are genuinely good, somewhere between a blueberry and an almond, though birds almost always get there first.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with darker vertical striping
pest_resistance: Cedar-serviceberry rust; generally easy
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; sun to part shade
description: Among the first native trees to flower, in a haze of white before the leaves. The June berries are edible and much loved by birds.
fun_fact: Also called serviceberry: it blooms when the ground has thawed enough for burials, and for the circuit preacher to reach the settlements.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey, striped darker
pest_resistance: Rust and leaf spot; generally healthier than the parents
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acidic
description: A hybrid serviceberry with larger flowers than either parent, opening pink-tinged before the leaves.
fun_fact: A cross between two native serviceberries with larger flowers than either parent, which is what the name records.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with darker vertical striping
pest_resistance: More rust and leaf-spot resistant than most serviceberries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; sun to part shade
description: A serviceberry selected for heavy white bloom, edible June fruit and reliable orange-red autumn colour. Often grown multi-stemmed.
fun_fact: Selected for autumn colour that runs orange to deep red, rather than the yellow most serviceberries manage.

bark_profile: Pale grey and heavily armed with sharp prickles
pest_resistance: Few pests; suckers aggressively into thickets
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; sun to part shade
description: A gawky, sparsely branched small tree armed with vicious prickles, carrying enormous compound leaves and frothy late-summer flower heads.
fun_fact: Its leaves are among the largest of any temperate tree, up to four feet long, and the trunk is armed with spines all the way up — hence the name.

bark_profile: Bronze-gold, shredding in fine curls
pest_resistance: Bronze birch borer on stressed trees
soil_preference: Cool, moist, acid; shade tolerant when young
description: Bronze-gold shredding bark; twigs smell of wintergreen when scratched.
fun_fact: Scratch a twig and it smells and tastes of wintergreen. Yellow birch is the longest-lived of our birches, sometimes passing 300 years.

bark_profile: Dark cherry-like with horizontal lenticels, plating with age
pest_resistance: Relatively borer-resistant
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; rocky slopes
description: Dark, cherry-like bark and twigs that smell distinctly of wintergreen when scratched — the original source of the oil.
fun_fact: Before wintergreen oil could be made synthetically, it was distilled from this tree's bark and twigs by the barrel.

bark_profile: Ragged salmon-pink and cream, peeling in sheets
pest_resistance: Resistant to bronze birch borer, unlike most birches
soil_preference: Wet to moist, acid; tolerates flooding
description: A river birch whose ragged, salmon-pink bark peels in sheets. Unusually heat-tolerant for a birch, and resistant to bronze birch borer.
fun_fact: The only birch that thrives in the humid Southeast, and the one birch reliably untroubled by the bronze birch borer that kills the white-barked kinds.

bark_profile: Peeling in wide sheets of cream, salmon and cinnamon — paler than the species
pest_resistance: Resistant to bronze birch borer and leaf spot
soil_preference: Moist to wet, acid; tolerates flooding
description: A river birch selected for lighter, showier peeling bark and cleaner foliage. The usual choice where white birches would fail to borers.
fun_fact: Selected for bark that peels away pale cream and salmon rather than the species' cinnamon brown.

bark_profile: Chalk-white, peeling in wide papery sheets
pest_resistance: Bronze birch borer is the usual killer of stressed trees
soil_preference: Cool, moist, acid; suffers in heat
description: White peeling bark makes this one of the most recognizable trees in Vermont.
fun_fact: The bark is waterproof, rot-resistant and peels in sheets, which is why canoes were built from it — and why peeling it from a living tree scars it permanently.

bark_profile: Chalky white and non-peeling, with dark triangles under branches
pest_resistance: Bronze birch borer; short-lived
soil_preference: Poor, dry, sterile ground; a pioneer
description: A slender pioneer birch of poor soils, with chalky white bark that does not peel and dark triangular patches beneath each branch.
fun_fact: A pioneer that colonises burned and abandoned ground where little else will start. Its bark does not peel in sheets like paper birch.

bark_profile: Chalky non-peeling white with dark triangles beneath the branches
pest_resistance: Selected for bronze birch borer resistance, the usual killer of white birches
soil_preference: Tolerates heat and poorer soil better than paper birch
description: A grey birch selection with a single straight trunk and chalk-white bark that does not peel. Chosen for borer resistance where paper birch struggles.
fun_fact: Selected for chalk-white bark and resistance to the bronze birch borer, which limits how long a white birch lasts this far south.

bark_profile: Pale grey-brown, corky on old stems
pest_resistance: Boxwood blight, leafminer and winter burn on exposed sites
soil_preference: Well-drained, neutral to alkaline; shallow-rooted
description: The classic clipped evergreen of formal gardens. Small leathery leaves, and a distinctive scent that people either like or very much do not.
fun_fact: Boxwood is so dense it sinks in water. Wood engravers cut their blocks from it because the end grain takes a line finer than any metal type.

bark_profile: Fibrous grey-brown, shredding in vertical strips
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Cool, moist, well-drained
description: A Pacific coast cypress with drooping, curtain-like sprays of foliage that give it a permanently wilted look.
fun_fact: One of the slowest-growing and longest-lived conifers of the Pacific coast; trees over a thousand years old are known.

bark_profile: Smooth olive-green, becoming grey-brown
pest_resistance: Very few problems; extremely tough
soil_preference: Poor, dry, alkaline; fixes its own nitrogen
description: A nitrogen-fixing legume from Siberia that survives cold, drought and salt where nothing else will. Pea-like yellow flowers in spring.
fun_fact: A legume, so it makes its own nitrogen, which is how it survives the Siberian steppe and the worst corner of a parking lot alike.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, fluted and rippling like muscle
pest_resistance: Very few known problems; among the most trouble-free street trees
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates alkaline soil, shade and hard pruning
description: A dense, fine-textured hornbeam that takes shearing better than almost any other tree, which is why it turns up as hedges, allées and narrow street forms.
fun_fact: The wood is so hard that mills cut their gear teeth from it. The name is horn, for hardness, plus beam, the old word for tree.

bark_profile: Smooth blue-grey, rippling like flexed muscle
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; shade tolerant
description: Smooth grey bark ripples over the trunk like flexed muscle, giving it the names musclewood and blue beech. An understory tree of moist woods.
fun_fact: Called musclewood: the trunk is fluted and sinewy, as though the bark were stretched over a flexed forearm.

bark_profile: Grey, smooth at first, later shallowly ridged in a flat network
pest_resistance: Few serious problems; difficult to transplant
soil_preference: Moist, rich bottomland; tolerates periodic flooding
description: Named for the bright sulphur-yellow winter buds, the surest way to identify it. Nuts are too bitter for anything but squirrels.
fun_fact: The nuts are too bitter for anyone to eat, but the oil pressed from them once burned in lamps.

bark_profile: Grey, tight and ridged, not shaggy
pest_resistance: Hickory bark beetle; difficult to transplant
soil_preference: Dry upland slopes, well-drained
description: A hickory of dry upland slopes, with compound leaves that turn clear gold and a thin-husked nut that squirrels open readily.
fun_fact: Named because the nuts were thought fit for pigs and not much else, though squirrels disagree.

bark_profile: Grey, splitting into long plates that curl away at both ends
pest_resistance: Few serious problems; slow to establish after transplanting
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained
description: Unmistakable in winter for its shaggy bark peeling away in long curling plates. Sweet edible nuts.
fun_fact: The shaggy plates that curl away from the trunk are prime summer roosts for bats, including the endangered Indiana bat.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly furrowed; rarely seen mature since the blight
pest_resistance: Chestnut blight is usually fatal before the tree reaches maturity
soil_preference: Well-drained, acidic; dislikes lime
description: Once the dominant tree of the eastern forest, reduced to stump sprouts by a fungal blight after 1904. Surviving specimens are worth recording.
fun_fact: A blight introduced around 1904 killed some four billion of these trees in fifty years. The roots survive and still send up sprouts, which die back before they can seed.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, ridged and scaly
pest_resistance: Catalpa sphinx caterpillar; large leaf and pod litter
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates wet and dry
description: Enormous heart-shaped leaves, showy white flowers in June, and long bean-like pods that hang through winter.
fun_fact: The foot-long seed pods give it the name cigar tree. The caterpillars that strip it are prized by anglers as bait.

bark_profile: Grey with distinctive corky warts and ridges
pest_resistance: Nipple gall and witches broom are disfiguring but not harmful
soil_preference: Very wide range; tolerates drought, wind and alkaline soil
description: Corky, warty ridges on the bark make this one easy to name by touch. Its small dark fruits persist into winter for the birds.
fun_fact: The purple berries are sweet and date-like, and stay on the tree well into winter as emergency bird food.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shaggy and peeling on older trunks
pest_resistance: Few pests; sensitive to drought when young
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, fertile; dislikes drought
description: Round blue-green leaves turn apricot in autumn and give off a distinct smell of burnt sugar or cotton candy as they fall.
fun_fact: As the leaves fall they give off a smell of burnt sugar — caramel, or cotton candy. Stand under one in October and you will notice it before you see the tree.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown, becoming scaly with orange in the fissures
pest_resistance: Canker; verticillium wilt; short-lived
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; part shade at this latitude
description: Magenta-pink flowers erupt directly from bare branches in spring, before the heart-shaped leaves appear.
fun_fact: The flowers burst straight out of the bark and even the trunk, a habit called cauliflory that is common in the tropics and rare here. They are edible, and taste faintly of peas.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown, becoming scaly with orange in the fissures
pest_resistance: Canker; at the cold edge of redbud's range here — site it with shelter
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; part shade at this latitude
description: A redbud whose new leaves emerge burgundy and mature through orange and yellow to green, so several colours show at once. Magenta flowers on bare branches first.
fun_fact: New leaves come out burgundy and age through orange and yellow to green, so the whole range sits on the tree at once.

bark_profile: Fibrous grey-brown, shredding in vertical strips
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Cool, moist, well-drained
description: The same Pacific coast cypress as Callitropsis nootkatensis under an older name — a species that has moved between genera repeatedly.
fun_fact: Its wood is fine, strong and rot-resistant, and was the first choice for canoe paddles and carving on the Northwest coast.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, peeling in long strips
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; shelter from wind
description: A Japanese cypress with fans of blunt, glossy foliage marked underneath by white Y-shaped lines. Sacred timber in Japan.
fun_fact: Hinoki is the sacred timber of Japan, reserved for shrines and temples; a Noh stage is traditionally built of nothing else.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, shredding vertically
pest_resistance: Blight in humid crowded plantings
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid
description: Japanese cypress grown in many forms, from feathery threadleaf cultivars to soft moss-like mounds.
fun_fact: Many of its garden forms are stuck in juvenile foliage — soft and feathery rather than scaled — a condition the species outgrows in the wild.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, peeling in flakes on older trunks
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acidic; full sun for best flowering
description: Smothered in fleecy white flower panicles in late spring, the whole crown appearing to have been snowed on.
fun_fact: A member of the olive family, which shows in the small blue-black fruit that follows the fringed flowers.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown, ridged with age
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, acidic, well-drained
description: Fringe-like white flowers hang in loose drooping clusters, faintly fragrant. Slow, and among the last trees to leaf out in spring.
fun_fact: Called old man's beard for the drooping fringe of flowers. Male and female flowers are on separate trees, and only the females fruit.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, beech-like
pest_resistance: Weak branch unions — needs early structural pruning
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates alkaline soil
description: Smooth grey bark like a beech, bright yellow autumn colour, and long chains of white pea flowers in early summer — though not every year.
fun_fact: Rare in the wild and scattered across a handful of states, yet perfectly happy in cultivation. The heartwood yields a clear yellow dye, which names it.

bark_profile: Slender grey-brown stems, exfoliating slightly
pest_resistance: Very few problems; spider mite in dry sites
soil_preference: Moist to wet, acidic; tolerates shade and salt spray
description: Spikes of intensely sweet white flowers in high summer, when almost nothing else is blooming. Tolerates wet ground and shade.
fun_fact: One of very few shrubs that flowers in deep summer shade, and the scent carries far enough that you smell it before you find it.

bark_profile: Smooth greenish-grey with pale striping
pest_resistance: Golden canker can kill branches or whole plants
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; part shade
description: Horizontal tiered branching gives this understory species its common name.
fun_fact: The only dogwood with alternate leaves rather than opposite ones, and the tiered horizontal branching that names it is visible from across a lawn.

bark_profile: Blocky, finely checkered, alligator-hide
pest_resistance: Dogwood anthracnose has reduced this species across its range; borers
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; part shade
description: Four large white bracts surround the true flowers, opening before the leaves. Under pressure from dogwood anthracnose across its range.
fun_fact: The four white petals are not petals. They are bracts — modified leaves — and the actual flowers are the small green cluster at the centre.

bark_profile: Mottled and exfoliating in tan, grey and brown patches
pest_resistance: Notably more anthracnose-resistant than the native dogwood
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid
description: A later-flowering Asian dogwood with pointed white bracts, raspberry-like fruit, and mottled bark on older trunks.
fun_fact: Its bracts come to a point where flowering dogwood's are notched. The fruit looks like a small raspberry and is edible, if bland.

bark_profile: Flaking grey-brown, exposing orange beneath
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates alkaline soil
description: Clusters of small yellow flowers on bare twigs in very early spring, followed by tart red fruit used for preserves in eastern Europe.
fun_fact: Among the first things to flower here, yellow on bare twigs in March. The tart red fruit has been made into preserves in eastern Europe for centuries.

bark_profile: Deep red young stems, greying with age
pest_resistance: Leaf spot and canker on crowded plants
soil_preference: Wet to moist; excellent for streambanks and rain gardens
description: A thicket-forming native shrub grown for red winter stems, and one of the most useful plants for stabilising wet ground.
fun_fact: The winter stems are brightest on the youngest wood, which is why gardeners cut it hard to the ground every few years.

bark_profile: Brilliant red young stems — the reason it is planted
pest_resistance: Leaf spot and canker on crowded plants; stems need renewal pruning for colour
soil_preference: Moist to wet; tolerates poor drainage
description: A compact redosier dogwood selected for intense red winter stems and burgundy summer foliage. Cut old stems to the ground to keep the colour bright.
fun_fact: Selected for stems that colour red earlier and hold it later in the season than the ordinary redosier.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: A dogwood recorded without a species — anything from a flowering dogwood tree to a redosier shrub in a wet ditch.
fun_fact: The name may come from dagwood: the wood is hard and close-grained enough to be cut into dags, the skewers used for roasting meat.

bark_profile: Smooth brown with pale lenticels
pest_resistance: Eastern filbert blight
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates alkaline soil
description: Grown here as the contorted cultivar, whose twisted, corkscrewing branches are most striking once the leaves have dropped.
fun_fact: Every contorted hazel in the world descends from a single twisted bush found in an English hedgerow in the 1860s, propagated by cuttings ever since.

bark_profile: Pale grey-brown, corky and flaking in small plates
pest_resistance: Remarkably free of pests; resists eastern filbert blight
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates drought, heat and alkaline soil
description: A neatly pyramidal nut tree, tough enough for difficult street sites and almost never troubled by pests. Underused for how reliable it is.
fun_fact: Almost alone among hazels it makes a proper pyramidal tree rather than a suckering shrub, which is why it turns up on streets.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking on old wood
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt
soil_preference: Lean, well-drained; poor soil gives better colour
description: Airy plumes of spent flower stalks give the whole shrub a smoky haze through summer.
fun_fact: The smoke is not flowers. It is a haze of fine hairs on the stalks of flowers that never set fruit, and it lasts most of the summer.

bark_profile: Grey, scaly and flaking
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt
soil_preference: Well-drained, alkaline; drought tolerant
description: The American smoketree, rarer than its European cousin and better in autumn, when it turns brilliant orange and scarlet.
fun_fact: Its heartwood yields a strong orange dye, and the tree was cut almost out of existence for it during the Civil War.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly; armed with thorns
pest_resistance: More resistant to rust and leaf blight than most hawthorns
soil_preference: Dry, alkaline; very drought tolerant
description: A tough, drought-hardy hawthorn from central Asia with finely cut leaves and small dark red fruit.
fun_fact: Hawthorn thorns are modified branches, not prickles — which is why they are woody, sharp and impossible to rub off.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly, wild trees armed with long straight thorns
pest_resistance: Cedar-hawthorn rust; the thornless form is usual in planting
soil_preference: Well-drained; very tolerant of poor and dry soil
description: A tough, wide-spreading hawthorn with glossy leaves, white spring flowers and red fruit that holds well into winter.
fun_fact: The thorns reach three inches and point outward at every angle, which is exactly why it was planted as a stock-proof hedge.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly, with long sharp thorns
pest_resistance: Better leaf-blight resistance than most English hawthorns
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought and urban conditions
description: Single crimson flowers with a distinct white eye, unusual in a hawthorn. Fewer thorns than the native species.
fun_fact: Selected for red flowers with a white eye, rather than the plain white of most hawthorns.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly, with long sharp thorns
pest_resistance: Rust and fireblight; leaf blight in wet years
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought and urban conditions
description: The best hawthorn for fall colour — scarlet leaves over glossy red fruit that hangs well into winter. Thorns are long and serious.
fun_fact: The last hawthorn to bloom and the best for autumn colour, with scarlet haws that hang on well past the leaves.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly, armed with long thorns
pest_resistance: Cedar-hawthorn rust; fire blight; leaf spot
soil_preference: Well-drained; very tolerant of poor soil
description: Thorny small trees with clustered white flowers and red haws. Notoriously difficult to identify to species, which is why the inventory stops at the genus.
fun_fact: The fruit is called a haw, and the hedge it was planted as is where hawthorn gets its name.

bark_profile: Grey, flaking to reveal orange-brown beneath
pest_resistance: Good resistance to rust and fireblight
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates both wet and dry
description: Flaking bark exposes orange inner layers, and the persistent red fruit stays on the branches through most of the winter.
fun_fact: Its bark flakes away to show silver and grey beneath, which is unusual in a hawthorn and the reason it is planted.

bark_profile: Thick, blocky, deeply checkered like charcoal blocks
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Wide range; very tolerant of poor dry soil
description: Blocky, alligator-hide bark and orange fruit that stays mouth-puckeringly astringent until it is thoroughly ripe.
fun_fact: The fruit is mouth-puckeringly astringent until it is properly ripe, and then it is superb. The tree is a true ebony, in the same genus as the black-wooded tropical kinds.

bark_profile: Shredding grey-brown, often multi-stemmed
pest_resistance: Verticillium wilt; canker. Invasive — spreads along waterways
soil_preference: Very tolerant of drought, salt and poor soil
description: Narrow silver leaves and fragrant summer flowers, but an aggressive invader of open ground and riverbanks. Mapped so it can be removed.
fun_fact: It fixes its own nitrogen and tolerates salt and drought, which made it a shelterbelt favourite — and then an aggressive invader across the western states.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, deeply furrowed
pest_resistance: Remarkably free of pests and disease
soil_preference: Tolerates a wide range including dry and alkaline
description: Tear a leaf slowly and fine threads of latex hold the halves together — the only hardy tree that does this. Exceptionally trouble-free.
fun_fact: Tear a leaf slowly in half and the two pieces stay joined by fine white rubber threads. It is the only hardy tree that will do this.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey, unfissured even when very old
pest_resistance: Beech leaf disease and beech bark disease — both present in Vermont
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; very shade tolerant
description: Smooth gray bark; a keystone species now threatened by beech leaf disease.
fun_fact: Beech bark stays thin and smooth for life, which is why people carve it — and why every carving is permanent, and an open wound.

bark_profile: Smooth elephant-hide grey
pest_resistance: Beech leaf disease; scale
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; dislikes compaction
description: The European beech, with the same smooth grey bark as the native species but usually a broader, lower crown. Purple-leaved forms are common.
fun_fact: Beech holds its dead leaves through winter on young growth, a habit called marcescence, which is why a beech hedge stays opaque in January.

bark_profile: Smooth elephant-hide grey
pest_resistance: Beech leaf disease; scale
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; dislikes compaction
description: A columnar European beech, the branches held almost vertically against the trunk. Smooth grey bark and a narrow silhouette.
fun_fact: A beech that grows as a narrow column, useful where the species' enormous low-branched crown would be impossible.

bark_profile: Smooth elephant-hide grey
pest_resistance: Beech leaf disease; scale
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; dislikes compaction
description: Deep blackish-purple leaves all summer, holding their colour better than most purple beeches before turning bronze.
fun_fact: Purple beeches all trace back to a handful of chance seedlings found in European forests in the 1600s and 1700s, and every one since has been grafted.

bark_profile: Grey with tight, regular diamond-shaped ridges
pest_resistance: Emerald ash borer — lethal without repeated treatment
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained
description: Under severe pressure from emerald ash borer; campus specimens are monitored closely.
fun_fact: Ash is the wood of baseball bats, tool handles and hockey sticks: it is springy, shock-absorbing and splits cleanly along the grain.

bark_profile: Pale grey, smooth when young, later ridged in a diamond network
pest_resistance: Emerald ash borer is usually fatal; also ash dieback
soil_preference: Deep, moist, alkaline tolerant
description: The European ash, with matt black winter buds. Like all ashes, now under sentence from emerald ash borer.
fun_fact: In Norse myth the world tree Yggdrasil was an ash. European ash is now dying across its range from a fungal dieback as well as the borer.

bark_profile: Grey-brown with interlacing diamond ridges
pest_resistance: Emerald ash borer — lethal without repeated treatment
soil_preference: Moist to wet; very adaptable
description: A tough, fast street tree now devastated across the region by emerald ash borer. Campus specimens are monitored closely.
fun_fact: Emerald ash borer, arrived from Asia around 2002, has killed tens of millions of North American ash and reached Vermont in 2018.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: An ash recorded without a species. Every ash in the northeast is now under threat from emerald ash borer, so these are worth identifying properly.
fun_fact: The paired leaf scars and opposite branching make ash easy to name in winter — which matters now that identifying them is the first step in saving them.

bark_profile: Grey, deeply furrowed into corky ridges with age
pest_resistance: Almost entirely free of pests and disease
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates salt, drought and city air
description: A living fossil with fan-shaped leaves that turn uniform butter yellow.
fun_fact: The only survivor of an entire order of plants, unchanged in the fossil record for over 200 million years. Six ginkgos a kilometre or two from the Hiroshima blast lived through it and are still alive.

bark_profile: Grey, deeply furrowed into corky ridges with age
pest_resistance: Essentially pest-free; a male clone, so no malodorous fruit
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates salt, drought and city air
description: A male ginkgo selected for a broad symmetrical crown and uniform butter-yellow autumn colour, which drops over a day or two.
fun_fact: A male selection, so it never makes the notoriously foul-smelling fruit — which is why almost every street ginkgo is a named male clone.

bark_profile: Grey, furrowed with age
pest_resistance: Essentially pest-free; male, so fruitless
soil_preference: Very adaptable; suits narrow tree pits
description: A narrow columnar ginkgo for streets too tight for a spreading crown. Same fossil leaf, same clear yellow autumn, a third of the width.
fun_fact: A narrow male clone. Ginkgo leaves all drop within a day or two of each other, so a sentry row goes from gold to bare almost overnight.

bark_profile: Grey-brown in long narrow plates, wild trees heavily thorned
pest_resistance: Honeylocust plant bug; mimosa webworm; canker
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates salt and compaction
description: Fine, ferny compound leaves cast a light dappled shade. Thornless forms dominate in planting; wild trees carry fearsome branched spines.
fun_fact: The wild tree is armed with branched thorns up to a foot long, growing straight out of the trunk — thought to be a defence against browsing mammals now extinct.

bark_profile: Grey-brown in long narrow plates, thornless
pest_resistance: Honeylocust plant bug; mimosa webworm
soil_preference: Very adaptable; a standard urban street tree
description: Fine dappled shade and no thorns; a workhorse of urban plantings.
fun_fact: Inermis means unarmed: a thornless form of a tree whose wild version carries branched spines a foot long.

bark_profile: Grey-brown in long narrow plates, thornless
pest_resistance: Honeylocust plant bug; mimosa webworm
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates salt and compaction
description: A vigorous thornless honeylocust with darker foliage and a more spreading crown, holding its leaves later than most selections.
fun_fact: Thornless and nearly podless, which is the whole reason honeylocust became a standard street tree — no spines, no mess.

bark_profile: Grey-brown in long narrow plates, thornless
pest_resistance: Honeylocust plant bug; mimosa webworm
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates salt, drought and compaction
description: A thornless, nearly fruitless honeylocust with a strong pyramidal form, planted where the litter of the species would be a nuisance.
fun_fact: The fine leaflets cast light, shifting shade that grass will actually grow through, unlike the solid shadow of a maple.

bark_profile: Grey-brown in long narrow plates, thornless
pest_resistance: Honeylocust plant bug; mimosa webworm
soil_preference: Very adaptable; a standard urban street tree
description: New growth emerges bright golden-yellow and fades to green through summer, so the crown carries two colours at once. Thornless and seedless.
fun_fact: New growth comes out bright yellow and ages to green, so the tree carries a gold halo at its branch tips all summer.

bark_profile: Grey, scaly, curling outward at the plate edges
pest_resistance: Remarkably free of pests
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates drought, alkaline soil and city air
description: Bare and gaunt for much of the year, hence the name. Huge doubly compound leaves emerge very late and drop very early.
fun_fact: Settlers roasted the seeds as a coffee substitute, which names it. Raw, they are toxic. The pods are so heavy that no native animal now disperses them.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, ridged and striped, flaking with age
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; part shade
description: White bell flowers dangle in rows beneath the branches in May, followed by curious four-winged dry fruits.
fun_fact: The white bells hang in rows along the undersides of the branches, so the display is best seen from below — which is where a path should go.

bark_profile: Smooth light grey-brown
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist, acidic; tolerates shade
description: Ribbon-like yellow flowers open in late October and November, after the leaves have dropped — the last thing to bloom all year.
fun_fact: It flowers in late autumn, after the leaves drop, and the seed capsules from last year explode at the same time, firing seeds up to thirty feet.

bark_profile: Tan, peeling in vertical strips to show pale wood beneath
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought once established
description: Fragrant white flowers in late summer, followed by showy rose-red sepals that outlast them. Exfoliating bark carries the winter.
fun_fact: It flowers white in late summer, then the sepals enlarge and turn cherry red, so the best show comes weeks after the flowers are over.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, deeply furrowed in a diamond pattern
pest_resistance: Thousand cankers disease; walnut caterpillar; juglone suppresses nearby plants
soil_preference: Deep, moist, fertile, well-drained
description: Deeply furrowed dark bark and aromatic compound leaves. Its roots release juglone, which suppresses many plants growing beneath it.
fun_fact: Its roots release juglone, which poisons tomatoes, apples and many other plants outright — a chemical territoriality called allelopathy.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, shredding in fibrous strips
pest_resistance: Cedar-apple rust; bagworm; phomopsis blight
soil_preference: Well-drained; drought and salt tolerant
description: A variable Asian juniper carrying both needle-like juvenile and scale-like adult foliage, often on the same branch.
fun_fact: Juniper berries are not berries but fleshy cones, and the ones that flavour gin come from a related species.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, shredding in fibrous strips
pest_resistance: Cedar-apple rust; phomopsis blight
soil_preference: Well-drained; very drought and wind tolerant
description: A narrow western juniper, usually planted as a blue-grey selection for screening and windbreak.
fun_fact: A Rocky Mountain tree that endures wind, drought and thin alkaline soil, and can live over a thousand years on exposed rock.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, shredding in fibrous strips
pest_resistance: Cedar-apple rust; phomopsis blight in humid crowded plantings
soil_preference: Well-drained; very drought and wind tolerant
description: A narrow, silver-blue Rocky Mountain juniper grown as a vertical accent and windbreak. Holds its colour through winter.
fun_fact: The blue is a wax coating on the foliage, thick enough to rub off with a thumb — the same bloom that sits on a plum.

bark_profile: Shredding reddish-brown
pest_resistance: Cedar-apple rust; bagworm
soil_preference: Well-drained; drought tolerant
description: Junipers recorded without a species. Foliage may be needle-like, scale-like, or both, and the berry-like cones are actually fleshy scales.
fun_fact: Junipers carry two kinds of foliage: sharp needles on young growth and soft scales on mature growth, often on the same plant.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, shredding in long fibrous strips
pest_resistance: Cedar-apple rust — keep away from orchards; bagworm
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates drought, salt and alkaline soil
description: Not a true cedar but a juniper, with shredding red-brown bark and dense blue berry-like cones. First tree to colonise old pastures.
fun_fact: Not a cedar at all. Its aromatic wood lines cedar chests and closets, and it was the standard wood for pencils until supplies ran short.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, ridged and furrowed with age
pest_resistance: Few pests; self-seeds freely and is weedy in warmer regions
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought, heat and alkaline soil
description: Large yellow flower panicles in midsummer, when almost nothing else is flowering, followed by papery lantern-shaped seed pods.
fun_fact: Yellow flowers in July, when almost nothing else is in bloom, followed by papery lanterns that hold the seeds — which is why it is also called golden rain tree.

bark_profile: Scaly grey-brown, furrowed with age
pest_resistance: Larch casebearer; canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; needs full sun
description: A European larch: a conifer that turns gold and drops every needle each November, standing bare through winter.
fun_fact: A conifer that drops its needles: they turn gold in November and fall, leaving a bare tree that looks dead until spring.

bark_profile: Thin, scaly, reddish-brown
pest_resistance: Larch sawfly; eastern larch beetle
soil_preference: Wet, acid, boggy ground; full sun
description: A deciduous conifer whose needles turn gold and drop each November.
fun_fact: Tamarack roots were used to sew birchbark canoes, and its wood is so rot-resistant that it was used for boat knees and fence posts.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: A larch recorded without a species. Conifers that drop their needles each autumn, turning gold before they go.
fun_fact: Larches are deciduous conifers. Turning gold and going bare in autumn is normal, not a sign that anything is wrong.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, deeply furrowed, twigs often corky-winged
pest_resistance: Chlorosis on alkaline soil; fruit is a litter nuisance
soil_preference: Moist, slightly acid; dislikes lime
description: Star-shaped leaves turning every shade from yellow to deep purple, corky wings on the twigs, and spiky seed balls underfoot.
fun_fact: The spiky seed balls are the reason it is loved and hated: the autumn colour runs purple, red and orange on the same tree, and the fruit ruins a lawn mower.

bark_profile: Grey with deep interlacing diamond furrows
pest_resistance: Aphid honeydew; sensitive to drought
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained; dislikes drought
description: Straight-trunked and tall, with oddly squared-off leaves and greenish-orange tulip flowers held high in the crown where they are easily missed.
fun_fact: The orange-and-green flowers are genuine tulips in shape but sit high in the crown, so most people never see one. It is a magnolia relative, not a poplar.

bark_profile: Grey with deep interlacing diamond furrows
pest_resistance: Aphid honeydew; sensitive to drought
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained; dislikes drought
description: Each leaf is edged in a broad yellow margin that pales to cream by late summer. Slower and smaller than the plain species.
fun_fact: Each leaf is edged in yellow, which lights the whole crown from a distance — unusual on a tree that grows this tall.

bark_profile: Grey with deep interlacing diamond furrows
pest_resistance: Aphid honeydew; sensitive to drought
soil_preference: Deep, moist, well-drained; dislikes drought
description: A columnar tuliptree, carrying the same orange-marked green flowers on a crown narrow enough for a street.
fun_fact: A columnar tuliptree, which puts the famously invisible flowers within reach of a second-storey window.

bark_profile: Shiny copper-brown, peeling on young trunks
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates poor soil, fixes nitrogen
description: A small, tough legume from Manchuria with upright spikes of dull white flowers in midsummer, when little else is in bloom.
fun_fact: A nitrogen-fixing legume that flowers white in midsummer, when almost no other tree does. The new growth emerges silvery grey.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown
pest_resistance: At the cold edge of its range here; winter burn likely
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; shelter from wind
description: Thick, glossy evergreen leaves with rusty felt beneath and enormous fragrant white flowers. At the very cold edge of its range here.
fun_fact: Magnolias evolved before bees existed, so the flowers are built to be pollinated by beetles — which is why they are tough enough to survive being chewed.

bark_profile: Smooth pale grey
pest_resistance: Enormous leaves shred in wind — needs a sheltered site
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, rich; shelter essential
description: Carries the largest simple leaves of any tree in North America — up to three feet long — and flowers to match.
fun_fact: The leaves reach three feet long, the largest simple leaf of any tree in North America, and the flowers can be a foot across.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: A magnolia recorded without a species, ranging from hardy star magnolias to southern evergreens that only just survive here.
fun_fact: Magnolia flowers are among the most ancient in the fossil record, built for beetles rather than bees, with parts that are neither quite petals nor quite sepals.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey
pest_resistance: Late frost ruins the bloom most years here
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; shelter from early sun
description: A shrubby magnolia covered in many-petalled white stars in very early spring, often before the last frost catches them.
fun_fact: It flowers so early that a warm March followed by a cold snap will brown every bloom — a gamble it takes most years.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey
pest_resistance: Few problems; late frost can brown the flowers
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, slightly acidic
description: Star-shaped white flowers cover the bare branches in early spring, before almost anything else. Hardier and more reliable than star magnolia.
fun_fact: A cross between star magnolia and Kobushi magnolia, made in Germany around 1910, hardier and larger-flowered than either parent.

bark_profile: Smooth silver-grey
pest_resistance: Late frost damages the flowers; scale
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid
description: The familiar saucer magnolia, with large pink-and-white goblets opening on bare branches. A hybrid raised in France in the 1820s.
fun_fact: Raised near Paris in the 1820s by a retired cavalry officer of Napoleon's, and still the magnolia most people picture.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly and flaking in irregular plates
pest_resistance: Apple scab, fire blight, codling moth — needs a spray programme for clean fruit
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The orchard apple. Vermont's cider and dessert varieties all belong here, descended from wild apples of central Asia.
fun_fact: Every apple variety is a clone. Grow a pip from a Honeycrisp and you get something else entirely, which is why apples are grafted.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly and flaking in irregular plates
pest_resistance: Susceptible to apple scab and bitter pit; needs a spray programme for clean fruit
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: A University of Minnesota apple bred for cold hardiness and an unusually crisp, juicy texture. Needs a second variety nearby to set fruit.
fun_fact: Bred at the University of Minnesota and released in 1991. Its cells are unusually large and break rather than tear, which is what makes the texture.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly and flaking
pest_resistance: Good resistance to scab, fire blight and rust
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: White spring bloom and small glossy red fruit that hangs well into winter for the birds. One of the more disease-resistant crabapples.
fun_fact: Named for the Arnold Arboretum's long-serving horticulturist. The bright red fruit hangs on all winter rather than dropping.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking on old trunks
pest_resistance: Good scab and fireblight resistance for a crabapple
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun
description: Deep carmine buds opening to pale pink then white, so the tree carries three colours at once. Tiny fruit persists for the birds.
fun_fact: The buds are deep carmine and open to near-white, so a tree in mid-bloom carries both colours at once.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly, reddish on young wood
pest_resistance: Notably resistant to scab, fire blight and rust
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: Deep pink spring bloom followed by small red fruit that persists into winter.
fun_fact: Selected for disease resistance first and flowers second, which is why it still looks respectable in a wet Vermont June.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, becoming scaly
pest_resistance: Among the most disease-resistant crabapples
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun
description: A low, wide-spreading crabapple, broader than it is tall. Pure white flowers and dark red fruit held into winter.
fun_fact: The smallest crabapple, wider than it is tall, named for Charles Sargent, founding director of the Arnold Arboretum.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, flaking on older trunks
pest_resistance: Excellent scab and fireblight resistance
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun
description: Sold as Golden Raindrops. Deeply cut, almost maple-like leaves and tiny golden fruit that hangs long after leaf fall.
fun_fact: Deeply cut leaves and small golden fruit, which is unusual — most ornamental crabapples were bred for red.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly and flaking
pest_resistance: Scab, fire blight and rust vary sharply by cultivar
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: Ornamental crabapples, planted in dozens of named varieties for spring bloom and persistent fruit. Recorded without cultivar in the 2014 survey.
fun_fact: Crabapple simply means an apple with small fruit. Every domestic apple descends from a wild crab of central Asia.

bark_profile: Fibrous reddish-brown, deeply fluted at the base
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Moist to wet, deep; dislikes drought
description: Known only as a fossil until living trees were found in China in the 1940s. A deciduous conifer with soft feathery needles that turn russet before falling.
fun_fact: Known only from fossils until 1944, when a Chinese forester found living trees in a remote valley. Every dawn redwood in the West descends from seed collected there in 1948.

bark_profile: Fibrous reddish-brown, fluted at the base
pest_resistance: Few known problems; foliage can scorch in full afternoon sun
soil_preference: Moist to wet, deep; dislikes drought
description: A slow, compact dawn redwood whose feathery foliage emerges pink-amber and holds a coppery cast all season, turning deeper before it drops.
fun_fact: A dawn redwood whose spring growth comes out amber-pink before turning green — and which, like the species, drops its needles in autumn.

bark_profile: Orange-brown, ridged and furrowed
pest_resistance: Fruit stains paving badly; weedy self-seeding
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates drought and poor soil
description: Introduced for silkworm culture and now widely naturalised. Leaves vary wildly in shape on the same branch, and the fruit stains everything.
fun_fact: Imported repeatedly to feed silkworms in failed attempts to start an American silk industry. The tree stayed; the industry never arrived.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, ridged and somewhat scaly
pest_resistance: Few serious problems; hybridises readily with white mulberry
soil_preference: Moist, rich, well-drained
description: Vermont's native mulberry, now scarce because it interbreeds with the introduced white mulberry. Sweet dark fruit stains everything below.
fun_fact: Native, and increasingly rare: it hybridises with the introduced white mulberry, and the hybrids are swamping it.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: A mulberry recorded without a species. Native red and introduced white mulberry hybridise freely, which is part of why the native is now scarce.
fun_fact: Mulberry fruit stains everything it touches, which is why the trees were planted well away from paths — and why fruitless male clones were bred.

bark_profile: Blocky, deeply checkered, alligator-hide
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist to wet, acid; tolerates flooding
description: Glossy leaves that turn the most intense scarlet of any native tree, often starting in August. Horizontal branching gives it a tiered look.
fun_fact: Among the first trees to turn each autumn, and among the most brilliant — scarlet by mid-September, weeks before the maples.

bark_profile: Blocky, deeply checkered, alligator-hide
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Moist to wet, acid; tolerates flooding
description: A tupelo whose new growth flushes bright red all season, on top of the scarlet autumn the species is already grown for.
fun_fact: New leaves emerge red and hold the colour into summer, so the tree burns at both ends of the season.

bark_profile: Shreddy, in narrow vertical strips that look cat-scratched
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Dry to moist, well-drained; shade tolerant
description: Called ironwood for its extremely hard timber. Shreddy, cat-scratched bark and hop-like papery fruit clusters in late summer.
fun_fact: The wood is so hard it blunts tools, which names it: hophornbeam, with fruit clusters that look exactly like hops.

bark_profile: Flaking in grey, green and cinnamon patches on older trunks
pest_resistance: Essentially pest-free
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates heat and drought once established
description: Tiny red flowers on bare twigs in earliest spring, spectacular autumn colour through yellow, orange and scarlet, and patchwork bark on old trunks.
fun_fact: The bark flakes away in patches of grey, green and cream, so an old trunk looks like camouflage. It flowers red on bare twigs in February.

bark_profile: Thick, deeply ridged and corky, soft to the touch
pest_resistance: Very few problems; female trees seed aggressively
soil_preference: Wide range; drought and pollution tolerant
description: The corky bark is soft enough to dent with a thumbnail. Male trees are planted because the females seed themselves into woodland.
fun_fact: The bark is thick, deeply corky and soft enough to dent with a thumbnail, which is what the name records.

bark_profile: Thin, coppery and flaking when young, becoming scaly grey-brown
pest_resistance: Spruce budworm; needlecast in crowded plantings
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; dislikes heat and drought
description: European spruce with drooping branchlets and very long cones.
fun_fact: The oldest known clonal tree on earth is a Norway spruce in Sweden whose root system has been dated at over 9,500 years.

bark_profile: Thin, scaly, ash-brown
pest_resistance: Spruce budworm; yellowheaded sawfly
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates cold and wind
description: A native northern spruce with stiff blue-green needles that smell unpleasantly of cat when crushed, earning it the name skunk spruce.
fun_fact: Crushed needles smell sharply of cat, which is why it is sometimes called skunk spruce — the quickest way to separate it from red spruce.

bark_profile: Furrowed grey, thick with age
pest_resistance: Rhizosphaera needlecast and cytospora canker are both common here
soil_preference: Well-drained; drought tolerant
description: The blue spruce of front lawns, with rigid, viciously sharp needles and a strongly conical outline.
fun_fact: The blue is a wax bloom on the needles that can be rubbed off with a finger. Seedlings vary from green to silver, so blue ones are grafted or carefully selected.

bark_profile: Red-brown, flaking in thin scales
pest_resistance: Sensitive to acid deposition and drought
soil_preference: Cool, moist, acidic; shallow-rooted
description: A spruce of cold Vermont uplands, its wood historically the first choice for violin and guitar soundboards.
fun_fact: The tonewood of choice for violin and guitar soundboards, cut from slow-grown trees with extremely even rings.

bark_profile: Scaly grey-brown
pest_resistance: Needlecast; spruce budworm
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid
description: Spruces recorded without a species. All have short, stiff, four-sided needles set on small woody pegs that stay behind when a needle drops.
fun_fact: Roll a needle between your fingers: spruce needles are square and roll easily, fir needles are flat and will not.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, scaly and flaking
pest_resistance: Few problems; scale and sawfly occasionally
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates poor and alkaline soils
description: A shrubby alpine pine forming a dense low mound. Size varies wildly between seed sources, so check what was actually planted.
fun_fact: An alpine pine from the European mountains that stays a sprawling shrub, which is why it ends up in foundation plantings.

bark_profile: Dark grey with pale plates
pest_resistance: Diplodia tip blight is common and disfiguring
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates salt and city air
description: A dense, dark European pine with long stiff needles in pairs. Tolerant of salt and city air, so often planted along roads.
fun_fact: Planted across Europe to stabilise poor ground and stand up to coal smoke, which also made it one of the toughest city pines.

bark_profile: Reddish, flaking in flat plates
pest_resistance: Diplodia tip blight; pine wilt
soil_preference: Sandy, well-drained, acid
description: Needles in pairs snap cleanly when bent, which separates it from other native pines. Reddish plated bark and a straight, clean trunk.
fun_fact: Despite the name its wood is not especially resinous; the red refers to the flaking orange-red bark of the upper trunk.

bark_profile: Very thick, deeply furrowed red-brown plates
pest_resistance: Fire-adapted and generally trouble-free
soil_preference: Dry, sandy, sterile, acidic — thrives where little else does
description: One of the few pines that sprouts new needles directly from its trunk after fire. Grows on sand and rock where nothing else will.
fun_fact: It resprouts directly from the trunk after fire, which almost no other pine can do, and its cones may need heat to open.

bark_profile: Smooth grey when young, deeply furrowed with age
pest_resistance: White pine weevil deforms leaders; blister rust
soil_preference: Well-drained, acid; intolerant of salt
description: Soft needles in bundles of five; the tallest tree in the Northeast forest.
fun_fact: The tallest tree in the Northeast. The Royal Navy marked the best of them with the King's Broad Arrow for ship masts, a grievance that helped stoke the Revolution.

bark_profile: Flaking orange-red on the upper trunk
pest_resistance: Pine wilt nematode; sawfly
soil_preference: Well-drained, sandy; drought tolerant
description: Recognisable at a distance by the flaky orange bark of its upper trunk and its short, twisted blue-green needle pairs.
fun_fact: Count the needles: Scots pine carries them in twos, with a blue-green cast and orange upper bark that no other common pine matches.

bark_profile: Flaking away in jigsaw plates to leave a smooth cream and white trunk
pest_resistance: Anthracnose in wet springs; powdery mildew
soil_preference: Moist bottomland; tolerates flooding and compaction
description: The white upper trunk is visible across a winter landscape. The largest-trunked hardwood in eastern North America.
fun_fact: The largest deciduous tree in eastern North America by trunk diameter. Old ones are commonly hollow, and were used as shelter — and once, famously, as a home.

bark_profile: Flaking in jigsaw patches of cream, olive and brown
pest_resistance: Anthracnose (less than the native sycamore); powdery mildew
soil_preference: Wide range; famously tolerant of city air and compaction
description: A hybrid plane tree whose bark flakes away in jigsaw patches of cream, olive and brown. Famously tolerant of polluted city air.
fun_fact: It sheds its bark in plates, which sheds the soot with it — the reason this hybrid became the standard street tree of London and Paris.

bark_profile: Smooth chalky white when young, becoming black and diamond-furrowed at the base
pest_resistance: Canker and weak wood; suckers aggressively from the roots
soil_preference: Almost any soil; very drought tolerant
description: Leaves are white-felted beneath, so the whole crown flashes silver in wind. Suckers so freely that it is difficult to remove once established.
fun_fact: The leaf undersides are covered in white felt, so a breeze turns the whole crown silver.

bark_profile: Grey-green and smooth when young, furrowed at the base
pest_resistance: Canker; borers; suckers freely
soil_preference: Wet to moist; northern river flats
description: Sticky, aromatic buds scent the air in spring — the balm of Gilead. A northern species of river flats and cold ground.
fun_fact: The spring buds are coated in a sticky, intensely fragrant resin that scents whole river valleys, and that bees collect to seal their hives.

bark_profile: Deeply furrowed grey, ridges thick and corky with age
pest_resistance: Brittle wood; cotton from female trees is a nuisance
soil_preference: Wet to moist floodplain; very fast
description: A massive floodplain tree with coarsely toothed triangular leaves that clatter in wind, and cottony seed that drifts in early summer.
fun_fact: The cotton is seed down, released by female trees in such quantity it drifts like snow — which is why only male clones are planted.

bark_profile: Smooth olive-grey, becoming dark and furrowed at the base
pest_resistance: Short-lived; canker and borers
soil_preference: Dry to moist, sandy or gravelly; needs full sun
description: A pioneer of cleared ground, with coarsely toothed leaves and the same fluttering habit as quaking aspen on a larger scale.
fun_fact: A pioneer of burned and cut-over ground that grows fast, dies young, and hands the site on to the trees that follow it.

bark_profile: Grey-black, deeply furrowed, narrow columnar habit
pest_resistance: Canker kills these young; rarely long-lived
soil_preference: Adaptable; used for quick screens
description: Planted as the Lombardy form, a narrow exclamation mark of a tree used for windbreaks and avenues. Short-lived and prone to canker.
fun_fact: Every Lombardy poplar is a male clone of a single mutant tree that appeared in Italy in the 1700s. None has ever set seed.

bark_profile: Smooth chalky greenish-white, darkening and furrowing at the base
pest_resistance: Canker; short-lived; suckers into clonal stands
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; needs full sun
description: Flattened leaf stalks make the foliage tremble in the slightest breeze.
fun_fact: The flattened leafstalk makes the leaves tremble in the lightest breeze. A Utah aspen clone named Pando covers a hundred acres and is a single organism.

bark_profile: Dark, lenticelled, becoming scaly
pest_resistance: Black knot; borers; short-lived
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun for foliage colour
description: Purple-leaved plum, grown for foliage rather than fruit. Pale pink flowers appear on bare twigs very early in spring.
fun_fact: Grown for the leaves rather than the fruit, though it does set small plums that are perfectly edible.

bark_profile: Dark, lenticelled, becoming scaly
pest_resistance: Black knot; borers; short-lived
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun for foliage colour
description: The darkest of the purpleleaf plums, holding near-black foliage through summer heat that fades others to bronze-green.
fun_fact: The darkest of the purpleleaf plums, holding near-black foliage through a summer that fades most of the others.

bark_profile: Red-brown, glossy, marked with horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Brown rot and borers; needs airflow
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun
description: The standard sour cherry of American pie, self-fertile and hardy enough to crop reliably in Vermont.
fun_fact: The standard American pie cherry, grown since the 1600s and named for a valley north of Paris.

bark_profile: Glossy amber-bronze, peeling in curls — its main ornamental feature
pest_resistance: Hardier and longer-lived than most ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; very cold hardy
description: Amur chokecherry, grown almost entirely for its glossy, peeling bark in polished amber and bronze.
fun_fact: The bark is polished copper-gold and peels in horizontal bands, which makes it a winter tree above all.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, smooth, strongly and unpleasantly scented when cut
pest_resistance: Prone to aphids and bacterial canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates cold
description: Long drooping racemes of almond-scented white flowers, unusual in a cherry. Bitter black fruit follows in midsummer.
fun_fact: One of the first trees to leaf out in northern Europe, with hanging white flower spikes rather than the usual cherry clusters.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, glossy, with conspicuous orange lenticels
pest_resistance: Short-lived by nature; black knot
soil_preference: Dry to moist; a pioneer after fire or logging
description: A short-lived native cherry that floods in after fire or logging, then gives way as longer-lived trees close over it.
fun_fact: Called fire cherry: its seed lies dormant in forest soil for decades and germinates en masse after a burn.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, marked with horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Peach leaf curl, borers and canker; short-lived here
soil_preference: Light, well-drained, sandy; needs full sun
description: Pink flowers before the leaves, and fruit only in a good year this far north. Reliably short-lived in Vermont.
fun_fact: Peaches came from China, not Persia. The name records where Europeans first met them, not where they are from.

bark_profile: Glossy chestnut-brown with prominent horizontal lenticel bands
pest_resistance: The longest-lived and most cold-hardy of the ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The hardiest ornamental cherry, with single pink flowers, polished mahogany bark and early orange-red autumn colour.
fun_fact: The hardiest of the Japanese flowering cherries, which is why it is one of the few that can be planted this far north with confidence.

bark_profile: Glossy chestnut-brown with prominent horizontal lenticel bands
pest_resistance: The longest-lived and most cold-hardy of the ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: An upright Sargent cherry narrow enough for a street, with the same single pink flowers and glossy mahogany bark.
fun_fact: A narrow Sargent cherry — the hardiest flowering cherry in a shape that fits a street.

bark_profile: Young bark dark with horizontal lenticels; old bark breaking into burnt-cornflake plates
pest_resistance: Eastern tent caterpillar; foliage is toxic to livestock when wilted
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, deep
description: Mature bark breaks into dark curling plates often likened to burnt cornflakes. Small black cherries in late summer feed most of the woodland.
fun_fact: Wilted leaves release cyanide, which has killed livestock that browsed a fallen limb. The wood is one of North America's finest cabinet timbers.
